Chapter 1 → Why Do People Become Entrepr.text: People start firms for three main reasons: to 'be their own boss' (the motive given most commonly), to 'pursue their own ideas', and to 'pursue financial rewards' — a motive usually ranked behind the other two and often a disappointment in practice. Public recognition is not among the three; most founders never seek the spotlight.

Chapter 1 → Be Their Own Boss.text: Wanting to be one's own boss is the reason founders give most often. Behind it usually lies either a long-held ambition to run one's own firm or frustration built up in traditional jobs — not any difficulty accepting authority, and not higher expected pay. Some people ease in gradually, operating the firm part time to gain experience and set aside money before they finally quit.

Chapter 1 → Pursue Their Own Ideas.text: Second is the desire to see one's own ideas realized. Established companies — which typically do give corporate entrepreneurs a channel for proposing ideas — often resist innovation, so good ideas go nowhere; some employees, driven by passion for those ideas, quit and build the business themselves. Outside corporate life, too, a hobby or everyday routine can reveal an unmet need, and when the idea can sustain a business, its owner pours enormous time and energy into founding one.

Chapter 1 → Pursue Financial Rewards.text: Financial reward is the third motive — and the most overhyped: on average, founders earn about what employees carrying comparable responsibility earn in conventional jobs, not more. What genuinely draws people is the 'upside potential' — a handful of founders have built billion-dollar fortunes. Money can also unify a team around a shared goal, yet it is seldom the main reason a firm gets launched; the boss and ideas motives rank ahead of it.

Chapter 1 → Characteristics of Successfu.text: Researchers have attached long lists of traits to entrepreneurs, but Figure 1.1 singles out four that successful ones share, in new ventures and established entrepreneurial firms alike: 'passion for the business', 'product/customer focus', 'tenacity despite failure', and 'execution intelligence'. General traits such as moderate risk taking, self-confidence, or being visionary belong to a separate, longer list (Table 1.3) — not to the four primary characteristics.

Chapter 1 → Passion for the Business.text: Of the four characteristics, passion for the business ranks number one. Belief in an idea is typically what launches a firm and what sustains its founder through rough stretches — Titin's founder said his conviction that 'there's a better way to train' both inspired the product and keeps him going. Passion has limits, though: enthusiasm must come with a clear view of an idea's flaws and risks, skills to match, and a legitimate business opportunity.

Chapter 1 → Product/Customer Focus.text: No elements of a business matter more than its products and its customers. Management, marketing, and finance all deserve attention, but they count for nothing when a firm's products cannot satisfy the customers they serve. The focus also shows in diligence — noticing product opportunities and carrying them through to a finished product, as the Macintosh team did in building the first user-friendly computer. Building the machinery of the business is a different characteristic: execution intelligence.

Chapter 1 → Tenacity Despite Failure.text: Trying something new means setbacks are unavoidable — building a venture resembles a scientist running experiment after experiment before one works. What separates entrepreneurs, the chapter's 'litmus test', is whether they keep going after failures. Yelp's founders passed it: when the original email-recommendation concept flopped, they kept the company alive and rebuilt it around user-written reviews, now among the Internet's most popular review destinations. Persevering after failure is its own characteristic, distinct from passion or product focus.

Chapter 1 → Execution Intelligence.text: Execution intelligence names 'the ability to fashion a solid idea into a viable business' — often the deciding factor between a start-up's success and failure. It covers the concrete work of company-building: designing the business model, assembling a new-venture team, raising the money, forming partnerships, keeping finances managed, and motivating employees — translating thought into action and measurable results. Generating ideas is not the skill; as Amazon's founder put it: 'Ideas are easy. It's execution that's hard.'

Chapter 1 → Common Myths About Entrepren.text: Misconceptions about entrepreneurs flourish partly because media coverage favors atypical cases — college students, say, whose venture-funded start-up reaches a valuation in the millions — while rarely noting that such founders are exceptions, and that their success came from carefully executing a sound plan built on a solid idea. Against that backdrop, the chapter corrects five widespread myths concerning what entrepreneurs are like and why they launch firms.

Chapter 1 → Myth 1: Entrepreneurs Are Bo.text: Hundreds of studies of entrepreneurs' psychological and sociological makeup converge on one conclusion: genetically, entrepreneurs are ordinary people. Nobody arrives in the world an entrepreneur; anyone can become one. Environment, life experience, and personal choice decide who actually does. The familiar entrepreneurial traits are acquired, growing out of a person's social context — children of self-employed parents, for instance, often come to prize independence, which is why entrepreneurship runs in families socially, not through inheritance.

Chapter 1 → Myth 2: Entrepreneurs Are Ga.text: Far from gambling, most entrepreneurs are 'moderate risk takers' — the same as most people. In The Hartford's small-business study, 79 percent of owners called themselves conservative, not risky. Neither are they risk-averse or impulsive; they occupy the moderate middle. The gambler image has two roots: founders hold less-structured jobs facing more uncertainty than managers do, and their strong achievement drive leads them to set challenging goals — behavior onlookers sometimes mistake for risk-seeking.

Chapter 1 → Myth 3: Entrepreneurs Are Mo.text: Entrepreneurs certainly want financial rewards, yet money seldom ranks first among the reasons they found firms or keep going. iRobot's founder described a mission that went beyond making money — to 'change the world in the process'; Ted Turner and Sam Walton both cautioned that fixating on wealth distracts, and that money was never what mattered most to them. Treating a payday as the whole story misreads what actually drives most founders.

Chapter 1 → Myth 4: Entrepreneurs Should.text: The Kauffman age table shows business ownership spread quite evenly across four major age bands from 20 through 64 — no band dominates — and most owners bring prior work experience. Nor do investors shun older founders: their most important funding criterion is 'the strength of the entrepreneur', and of the five qualities defining a strong one — relevant experience, a 'track record of success', useful skills, a 'solid reputation', and passion for the idea — all but passion favor age over youth.

Chapter 1 → Myth 5: Entrepreneurs Love t.text: A few founders are flamboyant, but the typical entrepreneur draws no public attention at all — many deliberately stay unnoticed because their products or services are proprietary. Consider how few people can say who founded Netflix, YouTube, or DIRECTV — services most of us use constantly. Entrepreneurs as a group crave the spotlight no more than anyone else, so a founder who avoids the press is entirely normal, not somehow less real.

Chapter 1 → Types of Start-Up Firms.text: The typology has three categories. Salary-substitute firms — dry cleaners, restaurants, hairstyling salons — earn their owners roughly what an employer would pay, selling common, readily available offerings; most small businesses are of this kind. Lifestyle firms — personal trainers, golf pros, tour guides — exist so owners can live from a 'sport, hobby, or pastime'; they neither innovate nor grow fast. Entrepreneurial firms create and seize opportunities to 'bring new products and services to market', giving customers value: 'worth, importance, or utility'.

Chapter 1 → What Is Entrepreneurship and.text: Entrepreneurship is 'the process by which individuals pursue opportunities without regard to resources they currently control'. Inventors stop at creating something new; entrepreneurs begin there — assembling and integrating money, people, business model, strategy, and risk-bearing capacity to make the invention a viable business. Established firms acting entrepreneurially practice corporate entrepreneurship, and every firm sits somewhere on a continuum from conservative ('wait and see', risk-averse) to entrepreneurial (proactive, innovative, taking calculated risks); that position is the firm's entrepreneurial intensity.

Chapter 1 → Senior Entrepreneurs.text: A substantial and rising share of people 62 and older are launching businesses. Three forces push the trend: corporate downsizing, a wish for greater personal fulfillment, and worry about paying for health care and other costs later in life — rising costs, not falling ones. Far from lacking preparation, many seniors carry decades of business experience, savings they can draw on, and good health, equipping them well to found firms across many industries. Life expectancy is rising, extending working lives.

Chapter 1 → Millennial Entrepreneurs.text: Millennials express high entrepreneurial interest — in one survey two-thirds wanted to start a business — yet only a small fraction of U.S. businesses are owned by people under 30. The biggest cited obstacles are lack of finances, lack of desire, fear of failure, and unfamiliarity with the start-up process; corporate job attractiveness, student debt, thin savings, and risk aversion also play a part.

Chapter 1 → The Positive Effects of Entr.text: Creative destruction is Schumpeter's name for the process in which entrepreneurs' new products and technologies gradually render existing ones obsolete. The stimulus comes from replacement, not from failures recycling resources or from predatory pricing: because the newcomers are typically better, their availability raises consumer demand, quickening economic activity and lifting society's productivity. Start-up ventures set the process in motion most effectively, and it reaches past products to new pricing strategies, distribution channels, and retail formats.

Chapter 1 → Entrepreneurial Firms' Impac.text: Entrepreneurial firms also make larger firms more effective. Some act as original equipment manufacturers, supplying the cutting-edge components and research behind big-brand products; many others build their entire business models around products and services that increase larger firms' efficiency or effectiveness, such as low-cost services large corporations subscribe to.

Chapter 1 → Economic Impact of Entrepren.text: Entrepreneurial firms strengthen an economy through two channels: innovation and job creation. Per employee, small innovative firms out-produce large ones 16 times over — and small businesses supply most of the country's net new jobs. A Kauffman Foundation study sharpened the job-creation point: a firm's age predicts it better than its size, with companies under a year old averaging 1.5 million new jobs annually across three decades while injecting competition and spurring innovation.

Chapter 1 → Decision to Become an Entrep.text: Step one revisits the three motives — being one's own boss, pursuing one's own ideas, and pursuing financial rewards — and adds that the decision usually waits for a 'triggering event': a job loss, an inheritance that for the first time puts start-up money in hand, or a lifestyle change, such as a parent whose youngest child reaches school age. The trigger is a personal circumstance, not an analysis step or an economy-wide process.

Chapter 1 → The Entrepreneurial Process.text: Four elements, in order, make up the entrepreneurial process: 'decision to become an entrepreneur'; 'developing successful business ideas' (opportunity recognition, feasibility analysis, business model, industry analysis, business plan); 'moving from an idea to an entrepreneurial firm' (ethical and legal foundation, financial viability, new-venture team, financing); and 'managing and growing an entrepreneurial firm'. Between the first two, the model draws a double-headed arrow: a promising idea can arrive first and itself prompt the decision to found.

Chapter 1 → Changing Demographics of Ent.text: Ownership is broadening: women, minorities, and seniors hold a growing share of America's businesses — women-owned firms, for instance, multiplied at roughly five times the national pace over nine years, and minority-owned firms climbed steeply too. The worry spot is millennials: their interest in entrepreneurship runs high, but the fraction actually choosing that path stays surprisingly small.

Chapter 1 → Developing Skills for Your C.text: Whether or not a reader ever launches a venture, studying entrepreneurship builds employability skills critical inside any organization: business ethics and social responsibility (building ethical cultures, Chapter 7), critical thinking (analyzing entrepreneurs' ineffective actions in the 'What Went Wrong?' features), collaboration (the 'Partnering for Success' features), and data literacy (gathering and interpreting competitor data, Chapter 5).

Chapter 1 → Women Entrepreneurs.text: American Express OPEN's study counted 11.3 million businesses owned by women in the United States as of 2016 — employers of nearly nine million people, producing $1.6 trillion in yearly sales. Growth far outpaced the market: women-owned firms were up 45 percent between 2007 and 2016, versus 9 percent for businesses overall — about five times the national pace. The separate 38 percent figure describes minority-owned firms, not women-owned ones.

Chapter 1 → Minority Entrepreneurs.text: The United States has eight million minority-owned firms, 38 percent more than in 2007 — growth the chapter calls encouraging. The 45 percent growth figure and the 11.3 million count describe women-owned businesses, a different statistic. Organizations that champion minority entrepreneurs, among them the Minority Business Development Agency, help sustain the climb.

Chapter 1 → Developing Successful Busine.text: Step two spans opportunity recognition, feasibility analysis, business models, industry analysis, and business planning. Two definitions matter here and are easy to confuse. A business model is a firm's 'plan or recipe' for creating, delivering, and capturing value for its stakeholders. A business plan is different: 'a written document that describes all the aspects of a business venture in a concise manner' — written, not an oral pitch, and usually needed for raising money and attracting quality partners.

source.authors: Bruce R. Barringer and R. Duane Ireland

learning_objectives.2.1: Explain the difference between opportunities and ideas.
learning_objectives.2.2: Describe the three general approaches entrepreneurs use to identify opportunities.
learning_objectives.2.3: Discuss the personal characteristics of entrepreneurs that contribute to their ability to recognize business opportunities.
learning_objectives.2.4: Identify and describe techniques entrepreneurs use to generate ideas.

Chapter 2 → The Differences Between Oppo.text: An idea is merely a thought or notion; it may or may not qualify as an opportunity, a favorable set of circumstances creating a genuine need for a new product, service, or business. A true opportunity has four qualities: attractive, timely, durable, and anchored in something that creates value for buyers. Its window of opportunity, the time when a firm can realistically break into a new market, must still be open. Many ventures fail because no real opportunity existed.

Chapter 2 → Three Ways to Identify Oppor.text: Entrepreneurs use three general approaches to identify opportunities for a new venture: observing trends, solving a problem, and finding gaps in the marketplace. Understanding all three matters, because an entrepreneur who knows each approach's profile is far more likely to notice opportunities and ideas that fit one of them.

Chapter 2 → Observing Trends.text: The first approach to identifying opportunities is observing environmental trends; the four most important are economic trends, social trends, technological advances, and political and regulatory change. Two cautions apply: distinguish real trends from fads, since new firms rarely have the resources to exploit a fad, and remember that trends intertwine — a product like the smartphone succeeds because several trends converge. Each category, studied carefully, points to gaps between what's available and what's possible.

Chapter 2 → Solving a Problem.text: The second approach is recognizing a problem and building a business around its solution. Problems surface by observing the challenges people encounter in daily life, or through intuition, serendipity, or chance; many founders first experienced the problem themselves, like the inventor of the insulating coffee-cup sleeve. Technology can create problems of its own for users it doesn't fit, such as seniors struggling with cell phones. Social ventures, for-profit or nonprofit, apply this approach to problems like poverty and hunger.

Chapter 2 → Finding Gaps in the Marketpl.text: Marketplace gaps are the third source of opportunities: products or services people want that aren't available locally or at all. Big-box retailers compete on price with mainstream merchandise, leaving room for boutiques, specialty shops, and e-commerce sites that serve narrower needs. Gaps are often spotted when a frustrated shopper realizes others share the same unmet need — as with plus-size fashion or guitars designed for women. A gap alone isn't enough; it must still be built into a successful business.

Chapter 2 → Prior Industry Experience.text: Research connects prior industry experience with recognizing opportunities: time spent inside an industry can reveal a niche whose customers go underserved, and the contacts made along the way may share insights that grow into ideas. Glauser makes experience one of his five criteria for start-up success; it also lends credibility with investors, customers, and partners. Still, experience isn't required — Uber's and Tesla's founders had none in their industries, and it can anchor a founder to a field's customary ways.

Chapter 2 → Cognitive Factors.text: Some believe entrepreneurs possess a sixth sense, entrepreneurial alertness — noticing things without deliberately searching for them. Such alertness is largely learned: the more knowledge someone has of an area, the more alert they tend to be to opportunities within it. Research is mixed, though; some scholars argue alertness involves purposeful effort, and that opportunity finders differ from nonfinders mainly in how well they size up the marketplace and infer its implications.

Chapter 2 → Social Networks.text: The breadth and depth of a person's social network affects opportunity recognition: research consistently finds that 40 to 50 percent of founders got their business idea through social contacts. The key distinction is strong versus weak ties. Strong-tie relationships — coworkers, friends, spouses — involve frequent interaction between like-minded people, so they tend to reinforce ideas a person already holds. Weak ties, the infrequent contacts with casual acquaintances, are more likely to spark a genuinely new business idea.

Chapter 2 → Creativity.text: Creativity — generating a novel or useful idea — underlies much opportunity recognition, and for an individual it unfolds in five stages: preparation (the background, experience, and knowledge brought to the process), incubation (mulling the problem over, consciously or not), insight (the eureka flash when the idea is born), evaluation (scrutinizing the idea's viability — a step many entrepreneurs mistakenly skip), and elaboration (working out the details into final form, such as a business plan). When stuck, return to preparation.

Chapter 2 → Brainstorming.text: Brainstorming is simply generating many ideas about a specific topic, from solo list-making to formal moderated group sessions. A productive formal session is freewheeling and fast-paced, and it is for generating ideas only — analysis and decisions come later. Four strict rules govern it: no criticism of any kind (even skeptical facial expressions), freewheeling is encouraged since wild ideas can lead to good ones, the pace stays quick, and leapfrogging from one idea to the next is welcomed.

Chapter 2 → Focus Groups.text: A focus group gathers 5 to 10 people chosen for their connection to the issue at hand — for example, a coffee shop's frequent customers. Through the give-and-take of group discussion, guided by a trained moderator who keeps things focused and lively, participants can surface ideas for new products or businesses. Focus groups are usually most productive as a second step, after brainstorming: they refine a general business idea that already exists rather than conjure one from scratch.

Chapter 2 → Library and Internet Researc.text: Library and Internet research is a third idea-generation technique. Choosing an idea first and only then researching it is too linear; the best ideas usually emerge when a general notion is combined with extensive research that sharpens it. Libraries are underused — reference librarians can point to trade journals, industry reports, and costly databases the library provides at no charge. Online, searching for new-business-idea articles, setting keyword e-mail alerts, and following industry experts on social media all feed the process.

Chapter 2 → Other Techniques.text: Brainstorming, focus groups, and published research aren't the only routes to ideas. Some firms keep a "customer advisory board": a standing panel of customers convened regularly to air what they need, want, and struggle with — recurring conversations that can seed new offerings. Others practice anthropological observation such as "day-in-the-life research": rather than asking questions, Intuit stations testers in customers' homes and businesses to watch its products in real use and draw product ideas from what they see.

Weeks later, driving home, the answer surfaced whole — refit the truck as a lunchtime soup line for office parks — and he spent two weeks checking whether the numbers worked before pinning down routes, permits, and a menu. shared_options.correction: a form of anthropological research in which a company sends its own people to users' homes and businesses to watch its products in real use and seek insights for new ideas

Which idea-generation technique is Leah using?

Over dessert, guests call out whatever concepts occur to them, each remark sparking the next; nothing is judged at the table, and Nkem sorts through the full list afterward. Which idea-generation technique is she using?

What fills the pad is the stack beside it — back issues of two pet-industry magazines, a printed market report on grooming and boarding services, and the morning's e-mail digest of industry news — and by each evening's end the page holds another column of possibilities, each one suggested by something in the coverage. Which idea-generation technique is she using?

source.authors: Bruce R. Barringer and R. Duane Ireland

learning_objectives.3.1: Explain what a feasibility analysis is and why it's important.
learning_objectives.3.2: Describe a product/service feasibility analysis, explain its purpose, and discuss the two primary issues that a proposed business should consider in this area.
learning_objectives.3.3: Describe an industry/market feasibility analysis, explain its purpose, and discuss the two primary issues to consider when completing this analysis.
learning_objectives.3.4: Explain what an organizational feasibility analysis is and its purpose and discuss the two primary issues to consider when completing this analysis.
learning_objectives.3.5: Describe what a financial feasibility analysis is, explain its importance, and discuss the most critical issues to consider when completing this analysis.
learning_objectives.3.6: Describe a feasibility analysis template and explain why it is important for entrepreneurs to use this template.

Chapter 3 → Feasibility Analysis.text: Feasibility analysis is the process of determining whether a business idea is viable — an investigative critique of a potential business, conducted after an opportunity is recognized but before a business model or plan. Passing requires a yes in all four areas (product/service, industry/target market, organizational, financial); a no in any one means drop or rethink. Mullins warns that skipping it invites the 'everything about my opportunity is wonderful' mode. It uses primary research (firsthand) and secondary research (already-collected data).

Chapter 3 → Product/Service Feasibility.text: Product/service feasibility analysis assesses the overall appeal of the proposed product or service. Whatever else a venture gets right, nothing matters if the product itself doesn't sell. It has two components: product/service desirability — does the offering serve a need and appeal to buyers — and product/service demand — will enough people actually buy it.

Chapter 3 → Product/Service Desirability.text: Desirability asks whether the offering makes sense, serves a need, is timely, and has no fatal flaw. The key tool is a concept test: a one-page concept statement — description, target market, benefits, positioning, management team — shown to at least 25 people familiar with the industry. Family and friends are avoided because they are predisposed to positive feedback. Iterating toward product/market fit — 'Have I built something people want?' — is the goal.

Chapter 3 → Product/Service Demand.text: Demand is assessed three ways: talking face-to-face with potential customers (the only way to know what people want — and the customer is whoever pays the bill, which in health care is often an insurer or Medicare, not the patient); online tools such as surveys, Q&A sites, and AdWords-plus-landing-page tests; and library, Internet, and gumshoe research. Surveys validate what interviews have already revealed rather than collect initial data; confirmation bias — searching for validating information — must be guarded against.

Chapter 3 → Prototyping: How to Build Wh.text: A prototype is an early sample or model built to test a concept. Iterative prototyping — 'fail early and often' — runs many small tests with potential customers, discarding what they dislike and building on what they like. The toaster example proceeds from a simple drawing with a description, to an inexpensive mock-up placed in real homes, to CAD drawings producing a sophisticated prototype. The goal is the version customers want, not the version you set out to build.

Chapter 3 → Industry/Target Market Feasi.text: Industry/target market feasibility weighs the appeal of both the arena and the slice of it the venture would serve. The two differ: an industry is 'a group of firms producing a similar product or service' — producers, not customers or territory — while a firm's target market is 'the portion of the industry that it goes after'. Start-ups rarely chase whole industries; they pick one narrow customer group to serve exceptionally well. Its two components: industry attractiveness and target market attractiveness.

Chapter 3 → Industry Attractiveness.text: Attractive industries are young rather than old, early in their life cycle, fragmented rather than concentrated, growing, not crowded, selling 'must have' products, with high operating margins and no dependence on a historically cheap input. Structural attractiveness matters: high entry barriers or one or two dominant players can shut new entrants out. The exception: older industries that haven't seen much innovation invite disruption — Warby Parker, Casper, Uber, ZenDesk.

Chapter 3 → Target Market Attractiveness.text: A target market is 'a narrower group of customers with similar needs' — a slice of a larger market. Start-ups seldom have resources for broad markets; a narrow focus avoids direct competition with industry leaders and serves a specialized group well. Pioneering product and market together is too costly, so start-ups typically pioneer one — a new product for an existing market, or the other way around. Assessing a pioneering niche requires synthesizing data from 'more than one industry and/or market'.

Chapter 3 → Organizational Feasibility A.text: Organizational feasibility analysis determines whether a proposed business has sufficient management expertise, organizational competence, and resources to launch successfully. It examines two primary issues: management prowess — the ability of the initial management team — and resource sufficiency — whether the venture has, or can obtain, the nonfinancial resources it needs to move forward.

Chapter 3 → Management Prowess.text: Founders should candidly assess their team's prowess. The two most important factors — with no practical substitutes — are passion for the business idea and understanding of the markets the firm will participate in. Additional factors help: extensive professional and social networks that plug knowledge gaps, and the ability to attract a capable new-venture team — the founders, key employees, and advisers who manage or help manage the business in its start-up years.

Chapter 3 → Resource Sufficiency.text: Resource sufficiency asks whether the venture has or can obtain the resources it needs — the focus is explicitly nonfinancial: office, lab, or manufacturing space; contract manufacturers; key employees with specialized skills (a local labor pool lacking them is a serious problem); essential equipment; the ability to obtain intellectual property protection (a quick Google Patents search shows whether someone filed first); and regulatory permission to operate. Firms list their 6 to 12 most critical nonfinancial resources and check availability.

Chapter 3 → Financial Feasibility Analys.text: Financial feasibility analysis is a preliminary financial assessment — detailed rigor is impractical this early because the business's specifics will evolve. The three most important issues are total start-up cash needed, the financial performance of similar businesses, and the overall financial attractiveness of the proposed venture. Complete one- to three-year pro forma statements come later, at the business plan stage, if the venture moves forward.

Chapter 3 → Total Start-Up Cash Needed.text: Total start-up cash needed is the money it takes to get the venture all the way to its first sale — not a guess but an actual budget: anticipated capital purchases plus the operating expenses of getting up and running, a serious account of where funding will come from, and a plan for repaying anything borrowed. Estimate high rather than low — the aim is surviving surprises: Murphy's Law thrives in start-ups, and unexpected expenses find nearly every new venture.

Chapter 3 → Financial Performance of Sim.text: Estimate a start-up's likely performance by comparing it to similar established businesses. Public-company data is easiest to obtain but such firms are typically too large for meaningful comparison; the challenge is finding small, comparable firms through industry databases, asking owners of similar non-competing businesses to share general figures, simple searches, and legwork — such as counting a similar shop's customers at various times of day.

Chapter 3 → Overall Financial Attractive.text: A venture's projected return is weighed against the capital invested, the risks assumed, and the existing alternatives for the money and for the entrepreneur's time and effort. A capital-intense, risky start-up promising a low return makes no economic sense, and someone leaving a $150,000 job requires a higher rate of return than someone leaving a $50,000 job. Other favorable marks include steady sales growth, recurring revenue, forecastable income, internally funded growth, and an available exit.

Chapter 3 → A Feasibility Analysis Templ.text: First Screen is a template for completing a feasibility analysis — named for the entrepreneur's first pass at judging an idea. It maps the four analysis areas; its final section invites revisions that can lift low-rated items, such as switching to contract manufacturing. Ideas at this stage are fluid: several versions cost little, while discovering infeasibility mid-plan or after launch costs much. Scores are a guide only — ranking an idea's potential is a judgment call, and candor is essential.

options: a short buying-intentions survey that measures how likely prospective customers are to purchase
a section of the finished business plan that describes the product line in full detail
a formal filing that establishes an entrepreneur's legal claim to a new product idea
a one-page preliminary description of a product or service idea, shown to others for feedback

items.stem: In the book Running Lean, cited by the chapter, Ash Maurya defines product/market fit as the answer to which question?
options: Can my product be produced at a competitive price?
Is my market growing fast enough to sustain a new firm?
Have I built something people want?
Can I reach customers at a cost my margins support?

items.stem: The chapter says a concept statement should be shown to at least 25 people who are familiar with the industry — and specifically not to family members and friends. Why are family and friends excluded?
options: Their enthusiasm tends to inflate the entrepreneur's ownership expectations
They lack the time to read even a one-page statement carefully
They are more likely than industry contacts to share the idea with potential competitors

False

Online surveys are too expensive for most start-ups to use during feasibility analysis

items.stem: According to the chapter, an industry is:
options: the portion of a market a particular firm goes after or wants to appeal to
a group of firms producing a similar product or service
the full set of customers who have ever bought a category of product
the geographic territory within which a firm competes

items.stem: According to the chapter, a target market is:
options: a segment within a larger market representing a narrower group of customers with similar needs
whatever group of customers a firm's established competitors have so far left entirely unserved
the complete set of buyers that a product or service could ever conceivably reach
a group of firms that produce a similar product or service, such as toys or computers

items.stem: Which of the following does the chapter list as a characteristic of an attractive industry for a new venture?
options: It is fragmented rather than concentrated
Its products are ones customers 'want to have' rather than 'must have'
It depends on the historically low price of a key raw material
It is late rather than early in its life cycle

items.stem: According to the chapter, why do most start-ups focus on a relatively small target market rather than a broad one?
options: Investors generally refuse to fund ventures that begin in large markets, where marketing costs cannot be forecast
Broad markets are almost always in the decline stage of their life cycle by the time a start-up notices the opportunity
A narrow focus lets a start-up avoid head-to-head competition with industry leaders and serve a specialized market well

False

Older industries are attractive because their incumbents have already proven that demand exists

The fee-based industry databases that libraries provide exclude niche categories from their published reports
Information from more than one industry and market must be collected and synthesized to make an informed judgment
Reliable data is published only for entire industries and is essentially never made available for any individual segment

items.stem: According to the chapter, an organizational feasibility analysis is conducted to determine whether a proposed business:
options: has sufficient management expertise, organizational competence, and resources to launch successfully
is preparing to enter an industry that is structurally receptive to brand-new entrants
offers a product or service that its prospective customers will find genuinely appealing
can raise enough capital from lenders and outside investors to carry it all the way to its first sale

items.stem: According to the chapter, a new-venture team is:
options: the full group of outside investors and lenders who fund a new business through the challenges of its earliest years
the group of founders, key employees, and advisers that manage or help manage a new business in its start-up years
the first paying customers a young firm recruits to advise it on improving its product
the panel of industry experts an entrepreneur interviews while conducting a feasibility analysis

items.stem: According to the chapter, the two most important factors in assessing management prowess — the ones for which there are 'no practical substitutes' — are:
options: prior start-up experience and a demonstrated record of raising money successfully
a formal business education and a portfolio of relevant industry certifications
an extensive professional and social network combined with a highly capable board of advisers
passion for the business idea and understanding of the markets the firm will participate in

items.stem: True or false: In an organizational feasibility analysis, resource sufficiency is mainly about whether the venture can obtain enough start-up funding.

False

items.stem: According to the chapter, a start-up whose business depends on a newly invented product can get a quick preliminary read on one key resource-sufficiency issue by:
options: hiring a patent attorney to prepare and file an application before any other analysis is done
deferring all intellectual-property questions until the business plan stage is complete
asking the established competitors in the field directly whether they hold relevant patents
searching Google Patents to see whether a patent has already been filed on a similar idea

items.stem: According to the chapter, the most important issues to consider in a financial feasibility analysis are:
options: the founders' audited personal financial statements, their past tax filings, and their credit histories

loan covenants, investor term sheets, and the likely timing of an eventual public offering
complete one- to three-year pro forma income statements, balance sheets, statements of cash flow, and accompanying financial ratios

items.stem: According to the chapter, 'total start-up cash needed' refers to:

the total cash required to operate the business through its first full year
the reserve a firm keeps on hand for unexpected expenses
the total amount of investor funding the founders hope to raise

items.stem: Which of the following does the chapter recommend for estimating the likely sales of a proposed smoothie shop?

Relying on the gut instinct the founder has sharpened through many long years of industry experience
Frequenting similar shops and counting the customers who come in and out at various times of day
Assuming sales will closely track the averages of large publicly traded restaurant chains

a feasibility analysis is an entrepreneur's initial pass at determining whether a business idea is feasible
it identifies and screens out the very first wave of competitors that a proposed new venture is likely to face
it was the first feasibility analysis template ever published for practicing entrepreneurs

repeat the analysis with a second, stricter template

learning_objectives.4.1: Describe business models and discuss their importance.
learning_objectives.4.2: Identify and describe the two general types of business models—standard and disruptive.
learning_objectives.4.3: Explain the components of the Barringer/Ireland Business Model Template that entrepreneurs can use to develop a business model for their firm.

Chapter 4 → Business Models and Their Im.text: A business model — a firm's "plan or recipe for how it creates, delivers, and captures value for its stakeholders" — is determined after the idea is validated and before operational details are fleshed out, never in isolation: founders should "get out of the building" and talk to potential customers. The model also maps how the firm's core aspects reinforce one another; the best are difficult to copy, and the more a model differs from competitors', the better a firm's chances.

Chapter 4 → Standard Business Models.text: Standard business models are existing plans or recipes for creating, delivering, and capturing value; Table 4.1 lists common ones. Many predate the Internet — Amazon moved Sears's mail-order model online, eBay the centuries-old auction. Successful start-ups typically adopt a standard model and build on it. Every model has weaknesses: subscription earns recurring revenue but suffers churn, the subscribers lost each month. A model also reaches beyond the firm's boundaries, so partners must be given sufficient incentive to participate.

Chapter 4 → Disruptive Business Models.text: Disruptive models are rare: they follow no standard profile and are impactful enough to change how an industry or important niche does business. A new market disruption "addresses a market that previously wasn't served" — Google's AdWords qualified because small businesses, priced out of online advertising, could buy keywords for a dollar a day. A low-end market disruption exploits "performance oversupply" — incumbents have improved past what many customers need, leaving a vacuum for simple, low-cost models like Southwest and Ryanair.

Chapter 4 → Peer-to-Peer Business Models.text: Peer-to-peer businesses match individuals wanting a service with individuals offering it. Airbnb, Uber, and Lyft are worth billions, yet BlackJet, Ridejoy, and Neighborrow failed with the same approach. BlackJet's fees were steep, the need infrequent, and first-class seats substituted for it. Ridejoy grew too slowly for investors, faced free alternatives, and saw riders cut it out of payment. Few people wanted to borrow household goods from neighbors. The lesson: no model is a "homerun" regardless of circumstances.

Chapter 4 → The Barringer/Ireland Busine.text: The Barringer/Ireland Business Model Template has 4 major categories and 12 individual parts. Core strategy covers the business mission, basis of differentiation, target market, and product/market scope. Resources covers core competencies and key assets. Financials covers revenue streams, cost structure, and financing or funding. Operations covers product or service production, channels, and key partners. The template gives an entrepreneur room to describe a model, project it, and then revise and pivot until every part is settled.

Chapter 4 → Core Strategy.text: Core strategy describes how a firm plans to compete against rivals; its parts are business mission, basis of differentiation, target market, and product/market scope. The mission says why the business exists and what its model should accomplish, and is completed first. Differentiation — two or three points — is what makes customers choose this firm; state benefits, what the product does for the buyer, not features, since features rarely entice a purchase.

Chapter 4 → Resources.text: Resources are the inputs a firm uses to produce, sell, distribute, and service its offering. To stay competitive long term, the most important resources — tangible and intangible — must be both difficult to imitate and hard to substitute: Uber's 327,000 drivers, Zappos's service reputation. Resources accumulate over time, so record current holdings while keeping aspirational ones in mind. Core competencies are what a firm must be especially good at; key assets may be physical, financial, intellectual, or human.

Chapter 4 → Financials.text: Financials is the only part of a business model that describes how the firm earns money. Revenue streams are the ways money comes in; a firm may have one or several. Cost structure asks whether the business is cost-driven, minimizing costs everywhere as Warby Parker does at $95 a pair, or value-driven, like optometrists charging $400 to $800 for selection, fitting, and follow-up. Costs are mostly fixed or mostly variable, which changes what funding is needed and when.

Chapter 4 → Operations.text: Operations covers production, channels, and key partners. For production, name the general region of a contract manufacturer and the type of arrangement, not merely that one will be used. Channels describe delivery: direct, through intermediaries, or both. Warby Parker prices so low that its model only works if the firm keeps all the margin, so it sells only direct; GoPro, being value-driven, can share margins with channel partners. Key partners include suppliers who do work outside the firm's competencies.

source.authors: Bruce R. Barringer and R. Duane Ireland

learning_objectives.5.1: Explain the purpose of an industry analysis.
learning_objectives.5.2: Identify and discuss the five competitive forces that determine industry profitability.
learning_objectives.5.3: Explain the value that entrepreneurial firms create by successfully using the five forces model.
learning_objectives.5.4: Identify the five primary industry types and the opportunities they offer.
learning_objectives.5.5: Explain the purpose of a competitor analysis and a competitive analysis grid.

Chapter 5 → Industry Analysis.text: An industry is a group of firms producing a similar product or service. Industry analysis is business research focused on an industry's potential. Before pursuing an idea, an entrepreneur asks whether the industry is accessible, whether it holds markets that are underserved or ripe for innovation, and whether positions exist that escape the industry's worst features. Studies trace 8 to 30 percent of the variation in firm profitability to the industry a firm competes in.

Chapter 5 → Studying Industry Trends.text: Two techniques gauge an industry's attractiveness: studying trends and the five forces model. The trends that matter most are environmental and business trends. Environmental trends — economic, social, technological, political and regulatory — make an industry surge or wane, often more than the skill of the managers running its firms. Business trends are other advantages some industries can capture and others cannot, such as outsourcing work abroad or moving service functions online cheaply.

Chapter 5 → Three Ts That Are Important.text: Start-ups stay current and become known through three Ts. A trade association is an organization firms in one industry form to collect and share information, give legal and technical advice, train, and lobby together. A trade show is an exhibition where firms display products, study rivals, and network. Trade journals carry industry-specific articles and advertising; controlled circulation, open only to industry participants, assures advertisers their ads reach the intended audience.

Chapter 5 → The Five Forces Model.text: The five forces model is Michael Porter's framework for understanding an industry's structure. Its forces — threat of substitutes, threat of new entrants, rivalry among existing firms, bargaining power of suppliers, and bargaining power of buyers — determine the average rate of return earned by the firms in an industry or a segment of one. Porter argues profitability follows from structure, not from how glamorous or technical the product is.

Chapter 5 → Threat of Substitutes.text: Industries are more attractive when substitutes pose little threat — when products from other industries cannot easily serve the same need. Where close substitutes exist, profitability is suppressed because buyers refuse a high price; free or nearly free substitutes hurt most. How much substitutes bite depends on buyers' willingness to switch, which is why firms add amenities — quality, atmosphere, service — aimed at alternatives outside the industry, not just rivals, so customers stay even when prices rise.

Chapter 5 → Threat of New Entrants.text: Industries are more attractive when entry is hard. A barrier to entry is a condition creating a disincentive for a new firm to enter. Six sources: economies of scale, product differentiation, capital requirements, cost advantages unrelated to size, access to distribution channels, and government or legal barriers. Start-ups creating a niche must raise barriers of their own; expensive ones are out of reach and patents often do not apply, so nontraditional barriers such as first-mover advantage suit them.

Chapter 5 → Rivalry among Existing Firms.text: In most industries the chief determinant of profitability is competition among the firms already there; fierce price competition can push prices below cost and produce industry-wide losses. Four factors set its intensity: the number and balance of competitors, with price-cutting likelier when firms are similar in size and no leader exists; how much products differ; the industry's growth rate, since slow growth forces fights over share; and the level of fixed costs.

Chapter 5 → Bargaining Power of Supplier.text: Industries are more attractive when suppliers are weak. Powerful suppliers suppress profitability by raising prices or cutting component quality. Four factors raise supplier power: supplier concentration, when few suppliers serve many buyers; switching costs, the fixed costs a buyer meets in changing suppliers; the absence of attractive substitutes for what the supplier sells; and a credible threat of forward integration, the supplier entering its buyers' own industry.

Chapter 5 → Bargaining Power of Buyers.text: Industries are more attractive when buyers are weak. Buyers suppress profitability by demanding price cuts or better quality. Four factors raise buyer power: buyer concentration, when a few large buyers purchase from many suppliers; the importance of the item in the buyer's own costs, which sharpens price sensitivity; how standardized the supplier's product is, letting buyers play sellers off each other; and a credible threat of backward integration.

Chapter 5 → The Value of the Five Forces.text: The model does two jobs: judging whether to enter an industry and whether an attractive position can be carved out there. Rate each force's threat as low, medium, or high; several high threats argue for reconsidering entry or rethinking the position. Four questions follow: is the industry realistic for a new venture; can the firm beat the industry at avoiding the forces; is a unique position available; is a business model available that incumbents could not copy?

Chapter 5 → Industry Types and the Oppor.text: Five industry types offer distinct opportunities. Emerging industries, where operating norms are unsettled, offer a first-mover advantage. Fragmented industries, made of many similar-sized firms, invite consolidation. Mature industries, with slow demand growth, repeat customers and little product innovation, reward process and after-sale service innovation. Declining industries, whose demand keeps shrinking, are met with leadership, niche, and cost reduction strategies. Global industries, with heavy international sales, call for multidomestic or global strategies.

Chapter 5 → Emerging Industries.text: An emerging industry is a new industry whose standard operating procedures have yet to be worked out. Whichever firm pioneers or leads it often captures a first-mover advantage — a "sometimes insurmountable advantage gained by the first company to establish a significant position in a new market." High uncertainty means any opportunity captured may prove short-lived, yet new ventures still crowd in because barriers to entry are usually low and no pattern of rivalry has formed.

Chapter 5 → Fragmented Industries.text: A fragmented industry is one made up of a large number of firms of roughly equal size. The main opportunity for a start-up is to consolidate the industry and become its leader. The usual route is a geographic roll-up strategy: one firm begins acquiring similar firms situated in different geographic areas. Businesses such as auto repair shops and beauty salons follow this path, since a single location can generate only so much additional income.

Chapter 5 → Mature Industries.text: A mature industry shows slow or no growth in demand, numerous repeat rather than new customers, and limited product innovation. Entrepreneurs occasionally introduce innovations that surprise incumbents who assumed nothing new was possible — soymilk entering the consumer milk aisle, for instance. The lure for start-ups is that these are often very large industries with vast potential if product or process innovation can be introduced and the industry revitalized.

Chapter 5 → Declining Industries.text: A declining industry, or part of one, is experiencing a reduction in demand. Entrepreneurs usually avoid such industries, though a start-up occasionally stakes out a position no one is contesting. Three strategies are employed: a leadership strategy, trying to become the dominant player, which is rare for a start-up; a niche strategy, focusing on a narrow segment that innovation might grow; and a cost reduction strategy, beating incumbents' costs through process improvements.

Chapter 5 → Global Industries.text: A global industry is one with significant international sales; many start-ups pursue foreign and domestic markets from day one. Two strategies dominate. A multidomestic strategy competes country by country, varying the offering to suit each local market. A global strategy uses the same basic approach everywhere. Which fits depends on whether tastes carry across borders: food preferences differ country to country, forcing the first; universal products like athletic shoes permit the second.

Chapter 5 → Competitor Analysis.text: Once a firm understands its industry and target market, the next step is a competitor analysis: a detailed analysis of its competition. It reveals where major competitors stand and where advantage is available. The work runs in order — first determine who the competitors are, then gather intelligence on their strategies and behavior, then organize what was learned in a competitive analysis grid.

Chapter 5 → Identifying Competitors.text: Identifying competitors is harder than it looks: a flower seller is also in the gift business, and defining the business more broadly brings both more competitors and more opportunities. Three groups exist. Direct competitors offer identical or highly similar products and matter most. Indirect competitors offer close substitutes meeting the same need. Future competitors could become either at any time. With no direct competitor, the status quo is the toughest rival — people resist change and can keep their money.

Chapter 5 → Sources of Competitive Intel.text: Competitive intelligence is the information a firm gathers to learn about its competitors. It is easier for public competitors, whose business and financial descriptions appear in filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission; private companies need not disclose anything. Ethical techniques include attending conferences and trade shows, buying and using competitors' products, studying their websites and social media, setting Google e-mail alerts, reading industry publications, and asking customers why they chose one product over another.

Chapter 5 → Completing a Competitive Ana.text: A competitive analysis grid organizes what a firm learns about its competitors. Competitive factors that matter in the firm's own segment run down the side; the firm and its main competitors run across the top; each cell records advantage, even, or disadvantage. Beyond showing standing and suggesting markets, its chief payoff is exposing where competitive advantage will come from; "even" cells mark room to improve. A viable new venture needs "at least one clear competitive advantage" over its major competitors.

source.title: Entrepreneurship: Successfully Launching New Ventures
source.authors: Bruce R. Barringer and R. Duane Ireland

learning_objectives.6.1: Explain the purpose of a business plan.
learning_objectives.6.2: Describe who reads a business plan and what they are looking for.
learning_objectives.6.3: Discuss the guidelines to follow to write an effective business plan.
learning_objectives.6.4: Identify and describe a suggested outline of a business plan.
learning_objectives.6.5: Explain how to effectively present a business plan to potential investors.

Chapter 6 → The Business Plan.text: A business plan is a written narrative, usually 25 to 35 pages, describing what a new business intends to accomplish and how. It serves two purposes at once: inside the firm a road map for executing strategy, outside it an introduction to the opportunity. Writing it is the last activity in developing successful business ideas. Writing one too early is a mistake: the plan needs detail accumulated during the feasibility analysis to convince a reader the venture deserves support.

Chapter 6 → Reasons for Writing a Busine.text: Two primary reasons. Internally, writing forces the founding team to think through every aspect of the venture, a discipline hard to find any other way. Externally, the plan is a selling document presenting the company to investors, suppliers, business partners, key job candidates and others. Its existence also shows the founder has thought each element through and was committed enough to do the work, and gives an investor something to react to. Surveys put formal-plan ownership at about a third.

Chapter 6 → Who Reads the Business Plan.text: The chapter names two primary audiences. The first is the firm's own people, the management team and the rank-and-file employees who must operate in sync and move forward purposefully. The second is the external stakeholders being recruited to join the venture: investors, potential business partners, and key employees. The two sections that follow take each audience in turn and set out what it wants a plan to show before it will commit anything.

Chapter 6 → A Firm's Employees.text: A clearly written plan articulating a firm's vision matters to rank-and-file staff as well as to the management team. Some argue planning wastes time because marketplaces change quickly; the chapter grants the point but answers that writing the plan can be worth as much as the finished document. A plan helps employees operate in sync, and is especially useful to a young firm's functional department heads, each of whom can check their own work against the firm's overall direction.

Chapter 6 → Investors and Other External.text: Investors, potential partners and key recruits are the second audience. A plan must be realistic — overly optimistic projections undermine credibility — and must show returns beating lower-risk alternatives. Many investors first request a one- to two-page executive summary or a PowerPoint deck; a full plan is usually required at due diligence, the investigation following a tentative commitment. Sophisticated readers want facts, above all the firm's own feasibility-analysis results and a distinctive, competitive business model, and expect every resource limitation disclosed.

Chapter 6 → Guidelines for Writing a Bus.text: A plan is often the first thing an investor sees, and an incomplete or sloppy one invites the inference that the venture is incomplete and sloppy too. Structure, content and style all matter. The chapter's red flags are founders with none of their own money at risk, a poorly cited plan resting on guesswork, a market defined too broadly, overly aggressive financials, and sloppiness anywhere. Each is read as a reason to doubt the entrepreneur.

Chapter 6 → Structure of the Business Pl.text: A plan should follow a conventional structure. Entrepreneurs who want to show creativity everywhere usually err by departing from it: investors are busy, want critical information where they expect it, and may give up and move to the next plan rather than hunt. Software packages can supply structure and save time, but a canned, boilerplate plan should be avoided and the content tailored. A consultant may advise but should never be the plan's primary author.

Chapter 6 → Content of the Business Plan.text: The plan should give clear, concise information on every important aspect, long enough to inform and short enough to hold interest. Twenty-five to thirty-five pages suits most plans, usually nearer twenty-five; supporting material such as the founders' resumes belongs in an appendix. Once finished it should be checked for spelling and grammar and for omissions. Plans have reached investors missing industry trends, the amount of money needed, even the entrepreneur's own contact details.

Chapter 6 → Style or Format of the Busin.text: A plan should look sharp without looking expensive: its readers know an entrepreneur's resources are scarce, and they expect spending to show it. The chapter's suggested binding is a plastic spiral binder with transparent cover and back sheets. Avoid overusing word-processing design features, which look amateurish. Three types exist: a summary plan of 10 to 15 pages for early-stage ventures, a full plan of 25 to 35 for investors, and an operational plan of 40 to 100 for internal use.

Chapter 6 → Recognizing the Elements of.text: A plan rarely stays fixed: it shifts during the writing and again as the venture develops, because immersion and early feedback bring new insights. The Lean Startup school opposes formal planning, preferring experimentation and customer feedback; this book argues the opposite — a new venture should begin with a feasibility analysis and then a plan, an essential starting point. A plan is not composed alone at a desk and left static; the research behind it keeps reshaping it.

Chapter 6 → Executive Summary.text: The executive summary is a short overview of the whole plan, giving a busy reader everything needed about the venture's distinctive nature. It is not an introduction or preface but a summary of the plan itself, no longer than two single-spaced pages, best written section by section in the plan's own order. Two identical versions are prepared, one inside the plan and one standing alone. Although it appears first, it should be written last.

Chapter 6 → Industry Analysis.text: The main body opens by describing the industry: size, growth rate and sales projections. It should treat the industry alone, not the industry and target market together. Industry structure means how concentrated or fragmented a field is, and fragmented industries take new entrants more readily. Most industries have six to ten key success factors every participant must be competent in, with participants differentiating on two or three. Trends and long-term prospects close the section.

Chapter 6 → Company Description.text: This section shows a reader you can turn an idea into a business. A brief history explains the idea's origin and the driving force behind its inception. A mission statement defines why the company exists and what it aspires to become, acting as a compass for decisions; a tagline reinforces market position. Products and services covers position relative to rivals. Current status is framed as milestones, noteworthy events already cleared. Legal status names the ownership form.

Chapter 6 → Market Analysis.text: The market analysis differs from the industry analysis: it breaks the industry into segments and zeroes in on the target market the firm will serve. Market segmentation divides a market into distinct segments, by geography, by demographic variables such as age, gender and income, or by psychographic variables such as personality, lifestyle and values. Buyer behaviour comes next, then a competitor analysis. The section closes by estimating annual sales and market share.

Chapter 6 → The Economics of the Busines.text: Revenue drivers are the ways a business earns money. Gross margin is selling price less cost of goods sold, the materials and direct labour to produce it; that figure is also the contribution margin, what remains per unit to cover fixed costs and produce profit. Variable costs move with sales; fixed costs are incurred either way. Operating leverage compares the two: high fixed costs mean a longer road to break-even, then more revenue reaching the bottom line.

Chapter 6 → Product (or Service) Design.text: Most products follow a logical development path: conception, prototyping, initial production, full production. The plan should say exactly where the offering stands and give a timeline for what remains. A product prototype is the first physical manifestation of a new product, often crude, made to gather feedback and iterate; a virtual prototype is a computer-generated three-dimensional image that can be rotated and viewed from every side. Challenges and risks must be disclosed honestly.

Chapter 6 → Operations Plan.text: This section outlines how the business will be run and the product produced, kept short and crisp because readers want an overall sense rather than detail. A useful frame separates back-stage, behind-the-scenes work such as staff selection, operations manuals, supplier relationships and training from front-stage activity the customer sees, such as tours, opening hours, staff assistance and classes. Business location, then facilities and equipment and how each is acquired, follow.

Chapter 6 → Management Team and Company.text: Many readers turn from the executive summary straight to this section, because funding often goes not to the best idea but to the team judged best prepared to execute. Each profile gives title, duties, previous industry experience, previous successes and education; gaps and the timetable for filling them should be named. A board of directors is elected by shareholders to oversee management; a board of advisors carries no legal responsibility and gives non-binding advice. An organizational chart shows accountability.

Chapter 6 → Financial Projections.text: The final section expresses the rest of the plan in financial terms. A sources and uses of funds statement says how much money is needed, where it will come from and how it will be used. An assumptions sheet explains the critical assumptions behind the statements, citing sources for the specific ones. The pro forma statements are usually built in sequence — income statement, then balance sheet, then cash flow statement — because each supplies information the next one draws on.

Chapter 6 → Presenting the Business Plan.text: A plan that interests an investor earns a meeting to present it in person, and the investor will usually want the firm's founders there. Investors end up funding very few of the ventures they see, so founders should leave the best impression they can. A first meeting is generally short, about an hour: a fifteen- to twenty-minute PowerPoint presentation, with the rest given to questions. An impressed investor asks the founders back to a longer second meeting with partners.

Chapter 6 → The Oral Presentation of a B.text: Follow the instructions given: that is the first rule — told twenty minutes, take no more. Rehearse until delivery is smooth, and keep slides sharp rather than cluttered. Arrive on time and prepared, having arranged beforehand any audiovisual equipment the investor may lack. Use plain talk and avoid technical jargon; founders often dwell on the technology and say too little about the business itself. Twelve slides suffice — a common mistake is preparing too many and rushing through them.

Chapter 6 → Questions and Feedback to Ex.text: Expect pointed questioning: investors can sound very critical, and discouragement comes easily, but an investor able to spot weaknesses in a plan or presentation is doing the entrepreneur a favor — that feedback improves both. First meetings turn on two things: is the opportunity real, and does the team have the skill and experience to execute? Investors also gauge the managers' confidence. The question period matters greatly; it shows how well founders think on their feet.

source.title: Entrepreneurship: Successfully Launching New Ventures
source.authors: Bruce R. Barringer and R. Duane Ireland

learning_objectives.7.1: Discuss the actions founders can take to establish a strong ethical culture in their entrepreneurial ventures.
learning_objectives.7.2: Describe actions taken in new firms to effectively deal with legal issues.
learning_objectives.7.3: Provide an overview of the business licenses and permits that a start-up must obtain before it begins operating.
learning_objectives.7.4: Identify and describe the different forms of organization available to new firms.

Chapter 7 → Establishing a Strong Ethica.text: Establishing a strong ethical culture is the single most important thing founders can do. A 2016 multi-country ethics survey measured four things: pressure to compromise standards, misconduct observed, whether observers report it, and whether reporters meet retaliation. In the United States 22 percent felt pressured, 30 percent saw misconduct, 76 percent of those reported it, and 53 percent of reporters were retaliated against. An ethical culture cannot be assumed; it must be worked on at every stage.

Chapter 7 → Lead by Example.text: Leading by example — the everyday conduct of entrepreneurs, managers, and supervisors — does more to build a strong ethical culture than anything else they can do. Where cultures are strong, those in charge communicate ethics as a priority, set a good example, keep commitments, provide information about what is going on, and support following organizational standards. Employees have their own part: consider ethics in decisions, talk about ethics while working, set a good example, and support following standards.

Chapter 7 → Establish a Code of Conduct.text: A code of conduct, or code of ethics, is "a formal statement of an organization's values regarding certain ethical and social issues." It gives entrepreneurs, managers, and employees specific guidance about what is expected of them ethically. Facebook's runs to thirteen sections and governs affiliates, subsidiaries, and others working on its behalf as well as employees. Other codes set out general principles. In all cases they aim to move people to behave consistently with the firm's ethical orientation.

Chapter 7 → Implement an Ethics Training.text: Ethics training programs "teach business ethics to help employees deal with ethical dilemmas and improve their overall ethical conduct." An ethical dilemma is a situation involving something beneficial to oneself or the organization that may nonetheless be unethical; most employees meet one at some point. Programs may be bought in or built in-house; one vendor's web-based course takes about forty-five minutes and teaches employees to recognize common issues and avoid acting unethically.

Chapter 7 → Choosing an Attorney for a F.text: An entrepreneur should select an attorney as early as possible. Two qualifications are critically important: familiarity with start-up issues, and a history of taking entrepreneurs successfully through the start-up process; a specialist is essential for intellectual property. Choosing someone merely because she is a friend, or prepared your will, is unwise. Ask the bar association for start-up specialists, interview several, check references, confirm a record of finishing on time, and discuss fees.

Chapter 7 → Drafting a Founders' Agreeme.text: Where two or more people start a business they should have a founders' or shareholders' agreement: a written document covering the split of equity among founders, how each is compensated for the cash or "sweat equity" put in, and how long each must remain for shares to fully vest. Most include a buyback clause obliging departing founders to sell their interest to those remaining, so shares can be offered to a replacement and stay with the committed.

Chapter 7 → Avoiding Legal Disputes.text: Most legal disputes come from misunderstandings, sloppiness, or simple ignorance of the law. Meet contractual obligations on time, and tell affected parties early if you cannot. Avoid undercapitalization: a business starved for money is far likelier to hit financial trouble that leads to litigation, so raise what is needed or slow growth. Get everything in writing. A nondisclosure agreement binds someone not to reveal trade secrets; a noncompete bars competing against a former employer for a period.

Chapter 7 → PARTNERING FOR SUCCESS: Vest.text: Instead of issuing stock outright at launch, a firm distributes it over time — typically three or four years — as founders and employees earn it. Schedules commonly run 36 to 48 months and include a twelve-month cliff: the time a person must work in order to leave with any ownership interest at all. Vesting keeps people engaged, fixes in advance how many shares a departing person keeps, and reassures investors, who dislike blocks held by former employees.

Chapter 7 → Obtaining Business Licenses.text: Many businesses need licenses and permits, which may be required at federal, state, and local levels depending on what the business does. Three ways to find out which apply: ask someone running a similar business; contact the secretary of state's office in the state of launch; or use an online search tool that searches by zip code and business type. The number-one rule is to ask when uncertain, since severe penalties follow operating without them.

Chapter 7 → Federal Licenses and Permits.text: Most businesses need no federal license, though some do. The chapter's partial list covers transporting animals across state lines, alcoholic beverages, aviation, commercial fisheries, drug manufacturing, firearms, wildlife, ground transportation, tax preparation, investment advising, maritime transport, mining, meat preparation, and broadcasting. Simple-looking businesses can need more than expected. Making beer that is sold requires a federal permit and a state liquor license; beer made strictly for personal consumption requires neither.

Chapter 7 → State Licenses and Permits.text: In most states three categories may apply. Business registration: some states require every new business to register, which records it, puts it on the tax authorities' radar, and prompts compliance with rules such as withholding taxes from employees' pay. Sales tax permits: most states require sellers of goods, sometimes services, to collect and remit sales tax, which needs a permit. Professional and occupational licenses: barbers, nurses and surveyors sit exams; plumbers and daycare centers need occupational licenses.

Chapter 7 → Local Licenses and Permits.text: Locally two categories may apply: a permit to operate a certain type of business — child care, barber shops, automotive repair, hotels — and permits for particular activities: building work, health where food is prepared or sold, signage, street vending, sidewalk cafés on city right-of-way, alarms, and flammable materials. Cities have quirky requirements, so check before launching. A fictitious business name permit allows trading under a made-up name. All businesses except sole proprietorships without employees need an EIN.

Chapter 7 → APPENDIX 7.1 Legal Issues In.text: Business names must generally be unique — usually no more than one business per name per state — and may not be confusingly similar to another's. To find whether a name is free, contact the secretary of state's office, typically online or by phone; if it is free, reserve it as that office recommends. Once an available name is chosen it should be trademarked, a straightforward and relatively inexpensive process given the protection it provides.

Chapter 7 → Choosing a Form of Business.text: A form of legal entity must be chosen at launch, and reviewed as the business grows: the choice is not a one-time event. Sole proprietorships, partnerships, corporations and limited liability companies are the usual candidates, and no single form works best in all situations. The decision typically hinges on four factors: the cost of setting up and maintaining the form, how far personal assets can be shielded, tax considerations, and the number and types of investors.

Chapter 7 → Sole Proprietorship.text: A sole proprietorship involves one person; the person and the business are essentially the same, and it is the most prevalent form. Set-up is cheap, the owner keeps complete control and all profits, and losses are deductible against personal income. It is not a separate legal entity: profit flows to the owner's return and the business ends at death or loss of interest. Unlimited liability and difficulty raising capital push entrepreneurs toward corporations and LLCs.

Chapter 7 → Partnerships.text: Two or more people must organize as a partnership, corporation or limited liability company. In a general partnership they pool skills, abilities and resources, usually with equal say; profits flow to personal returns; each partner is liable for all the partnership's debts; and it ends on a partner's death or withdrawal unless the agreement says otherwise. A limited partnership adds a second class: general partners bear the debts, limited partners risk only their investment unless they exercise significant control.

Chapter 7 → Corporations.text: A corporation is a separate legal entity organized under a state's authority, formed by filing articles of incorporation, governed by a board the shareholders elect, and shielding shareholders from its debts. A C corporation suffers double taxation: taxed on net income, then again on dividends. Neglecting annual filings or fees, or committing fraud, can lead a court to ignore the corporation and hold owners personally liable, which is piercing the corporate veil. A subchapter S corporation avoids the second charge.

Chapter 7 → Limited Liability Company.text: The limited liability company is a fast-growing choice for start-ups. Profits flow through to the owners' returns, avoiding double taxation, and every member enjoys limited liability, unlike partnerships where at least one partner bears the debts. Owners are members holding interests rather than stock; there is no ceiling on their number, and profits may be split in any proportions agreed. An LLC must stay private: to be listed it must first convert to a C corporation.
